articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved a lease agreement with Gulf South Towers to construct a 95-foot-tall telecommunications tower in the City’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. The new tower will be used by up to four wireless providers. The tower, base station, and other improvements were unanimously approved by City Council on April 19. The new “monopole” will replace an existing 31-foottall pole in the same location, currently with only one provider, T-Mobile. The city’s General Plan includes guidelines related to wireless communication facilities (WCF), and states that city staff must ensure “that the siting and design of infrastructure facilities mitigate the potential for adverse visual impacts.” The city’s Corporation Yard, located at 898 Red Rock Road, is located in a zone where telecommunications facilities are permitted without height restriction. The selected location was chosen because of natural “buffers” to the south, north, east, and west of the monopole. The visual impact and sight line analysis indicated that there may be minimal impacts to Bay views of some residences located directly to the east of the site, in Moraga Canyon, but that the impact is low. The lease agreement was approved by City Council in a second reading, following an approval by the city’s Planning Commission earlier this year. articles.text: Editor: I must take a contrarian’s view to the opinions in the May 12th Post of my friend of 40 years, Dr. Marvin Engel. Greta Thunberg is an enormously successful “climate provocateur.” The world is a far, better place because of her and her message. “Systemic racism” in my opinion is with us. I cite a few facts from the 2017 book by Richard Rothstein, The Color of Law - A forgotten history of how our government segregated America. When the WWII shipyards were built in Richmond the Federal government needed all the labor it could recruit to build those ships and get them launched. They thought nothing of putting black workers side by side with white workers. However, when they faced the need to build housing for all those workers, they decided they didn’t want blacks living with whites. So, the Feds deliberately segregated the housing. I know because my family and I lived in one of the whites-only units. In 1953 Ford Motor Company announced a new plant in Milpitas and the closing of the Richmond plant. The union negotiated an agreement that would allow the 1400 employees (about 250 of whom were African American) to keep their jobs if they transferred. The civic leaders of Milpitas quickly said there could be no new construction of multi-unit buildings – no apartments, no rentals. They also said only single-family homes could be built in the city. The union tried to intervene by building their own integrated subdivision for their members, but it was thwarted at every turn and was ultimately unsuccessful. Milpitas remained white. And let’s not forget the role of “red-lining”, that silent and nefarious practice to keep minorities from buying homes outside their segregated neighborhoods. Then there was the even more recent “reverse red-lining” in the form of predatory lending. It was at its worst during the run-up to the real estate crash of 2008 and included “excessive marketing of exploitative loans in African America communities”. These loans turned out to be disastrous for black homeowners. The Federal government gathered data from financial institutions that revealed this abuse but did nothing to protect minority borrowers. It was not until the Fair Housing Act of 1968 that decent homes started to open to black buyers. I have to believe all the unfair treatment and discrimination they have been subject to during my lifetime would lead them to agree that systemic racism is still with us. White young people and white adults need to better understand this so we can effectively remedy our history.
articles.title: Another history lesson of the Bay Area

articles.text: Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church was founded as the First Baptist Church of Brooklyn on the shores of Oakland’s Lake Merritt in 1860. Over the 161 years of our history, we have changed names (FBC Brooklyn, Tenth Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church). We also have changed buildings and have changed from being an almost exclusively white congregation to being one of Oakland’s most diverse congregations. In terms of race, we are approximately 45% African-American, 45% Euro-American, 7% Asian American, 2% Latino/a American and 1% Native-American. Our diversity is not accidental. It is a gift of the Spirit. It is the result of decisions made over many years. It is the result of making-mistakes and being willing to learn from them. It is the result of vision, courage, determination, resilience and repentance. It is the result of believing that, as we see in the eighth chapter of the book of Acts, Phillip from Judea and the Eunuch from Ethiopia belong in the same chariot, the same Bible class and the same waters of baptism. At this point I need to be very clear. We have not arrived. Many of the decisions listed above remain aspirational. We have much work to do. If we want to move from being diverse to being inter-connected, we have a training or two to participate in. If we want to move from being interracial to being anti-racist, we have some baggage we need to get rid of. If we want to move from being mono-cultural to being truly multicultural, there is some truth we need to hear and changes we need to make. These things can happen, but they won’t “just happen.” As we move forward, we have much to learn from the Bible. Biblical scholar N.T. Wright says it well. “The church was the original multicultural project, with Jesus as its only point of identity. It was known, and was for this reason seen as both attractive and dangerous, as a worship-based, spiritually renewed, multi-ethnic, polychrome, mutually supportive, outward-facing, culturally creative, chastity-celebrating, socially responsible fictive kinship group, gender-blind in leadership, generous to the poor and courageous in speaking up for the voiceless.”
articles.title: A word to a Church in formation

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s dream is also that of Shirley Hooi, as expressed in last week’s Piedmont Post. I was stunned by her naivete, confused by her assertions, and perplexed by her selective thinking. She said today’s “mainstream” ideology posits that “Whiteness” equals oppression and non-Whiteness as the oppressed. Certainly, such an ideology exists in today’s America. Rather than being “mainstream,” it competes with other ideologies in our hyper-polarized political culture, including Trump’s right-wing Big Lie and disharmonies among the many non-White, non-male communities. Remember, America was founded by wealthy White men, some of them slave owners. America has indeed progressed from those oppressive times, and it has been a land of opportunity for immigrants, despite institutional barriers. But as our population is becoming less White, portions of White America feel threatened. (See Trump’s insurrectionist supporters.) America’s racial-ethnic history isn’t glorious -- slavery, genocide of Native peoples, conquests of LatinX territories, the Chinese Exclusion Act, the Japanese American internment, and, today, anti-Islamic and anti-Central American hostilities. Ms. Hooi’s litany about America being the “land of the free, the land of opportunity” was muddled and confusing. She wrote, “…this is the land my ancestors fought to travel to and from during the Chinese Exclusion Act, this is the land that contained my ancestors on Angel Island…” Are these really “good” things about America? My parents and three older sisters, detained at Angel Island, felt imprisoned. She holds America “dear to my heart because of the freedom and opportunities that have been afforded my ancestors…” Her forbears must have been luckier than my immigrant father, who lived and worked in Oakland’s Chinatown, barred from “freedom and opportunities” because systemic racism kept him socially segregated, socioeconomically oppressed, and politically disenfranchised. Ms. Hooi worries that schools may implement Critical Race Theory (CRT) because, she says, “CRT promotes Whiteness as oppressive…” The CRT process will surely be politically volatile, but American schools must do better teaching all children the truth about America, the good, bad, ugly, and beautiful. Ms. Hooi urged people to speak out against her idea of “mainstream” ideology that, according to her, censures, ostracizes, and categorizes as racists or sell-outs those who go against “the tide.” That happens, as racial-ethnic issues persist as difficult, divisive, and daunting. I was stunned by her naivete, confused by her assertions, and perplexed by her selective thinking. She said today’s “mainstream” ideology posits that “Whiteness” equals oppression and non-Whiteness as the oppressed. Certainly, such an ideology exists in today’s America. Rather than being “mainstream,” it competes with other ideologies in our hyper-polarized political culture, including Trump’s right-wing Big Lie and disharmonies among the many non-White, non-male communities. Remember, America was founded by wealthy White men, some of them slave owners. America has indeed progressed from those oppressive times, and it has been a land of opportunity for immigrants, despite institutional barriers. But as our population is becoming less White, portions of White America feel threatened. (See Trump’s insurrectionist supporters.) America’s racial-ethnic history isn’t glorious -- slavery, genocide of Native peoples, conquests of LatinX territories, the Chinese Exclusion Act, the Japanese American internment, and, today, anti-Islamic and anti-Central American hostilities. articles.text: Crime is down slightly overall in Piedmont, according to the Police Department’s quarterly report on May 17. The city experienced a decrease in reportable offenses through the first quarter of 2021, compared to the same period in 2020, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers explained. A total of 78 reportable offenses in the first quarter of 2020 decreased to 73 reportable offenses in 2021. Motor vehicle thefts were steady both years, with 10 total reported offenses in the first quarter of 2020 and 2021. Burglaries, which the department defines as the unlawful entry into a dwelling with the intent to commit theft, decreased from 17 incidents in the first quarter of 2020 to six incidents this year so far. Robberies, which involve an individual stealing another’s belongings through means of force, increased from zero last year to two incidents in 2021. Larceny and theft, which includes breaking into locked vehicles, was up from 47 incidents in the first quarter of 2020 to 54 incidents in the first quarter of this year. Chief Bowers noted that there have been numerous reported incidents of vehicle break-ins throughout the city, which would be reflected in the second quarter crime report. The department continues to utilize Automated License Plate Reader cameras (ALPR) to address crime; Bowers explained that officers have made 13 arrests and have recovered 15 stolen vehicles in events directly related to ALPR cameras through the first quarter of 2021, compared to one arrest and two recovered stolen vehicles in the first quarter of 2020. A Request for Proposal (RFP) has been completed for the Public Safety Camera program. A recommendation will be made in the near future. Traffic safety The city continues to expand and maintain safe roadways for motorists, pedestrians and cyclists, with help from the Pedestrian and Bicycle Safety Committee. The Piedmont Police Department assists by conducting selective traffic enforcement targeted in areas throughout the city known for speeding and other violations, as well as in areas of high pedestrian traffic. Also, a traffic safety group of police officers works closely with the Public Works Department and city engineer to address safety concerns on roadways and at intersections throughout the city. Bowers noted that accidents doubled from last year, with 18 collision reports in the first three months of 2021, and nine the year prior. Of the 18 accidents, 12 were categorized as hit-and-run. articles.text: “Mr. Handsome” treated, then released into rural Santa Clara County A mountain lion that was captured and removed from a tree in San Francisco’s Bernal Heights neighborhood was brought to Oakland Zoo on May 20. It immediately received a complete exam, bloodwork, and preventative care vaccines. The two-year-old male nicknamed “Mr. Handsome” by zoo veterinary staff, and weighing 98 pounds, was released the following day into a rural area of Santa Clara County. San Francisco Animal Care and Control (SFACC) was the first agency to issue a notice post about the lion having been seen on May 19. At about 10:30 p.m., SFACC posted a photo on their twitter page of a mountain lion that was perched in a tree on Santa Marina near Mission Street. California Fish and Wildlife arrived at the scene and removed the animal from the tree after tranquilizing it with a dart. Data collected from the big cat’s radio collar revealed it was the same animal that Bernal Heights residents spotted roaming the streets in the two days leading up to his capture. KCBS radio reported that, after being shot with a tranquilizer in the hindquarters, the lion “got woozy and fell asleep on the front porch of a nearby home” before being tagged and caged, and then transported to the Oakland Zoo. “I felt frightened, but also somewhat giddy to have the worlds collide in this fashion, a beautiful beast like that living in the wild, yet wandering the city at night, looking for something to do and possibly a bite to eat - just like the rest of us,” said resident Ken Shelf who sent a photo to be shared with SF Animal Control. Veterinarians at Oakland Zoo explained that “long-range travel” into urban neighborhoods isn’t out of the ordinary for mountain lions. The species is known to travel long distances in search of food, shelter, and a mate. Luckily, the big cat received a total clean bill of health by the Oakland Zoo – strong, hydrated, and a healthy weight of 98.5 pounds. He was treated for internal and external parasites, which are common in wildlife, and was given preventative vaccinations during his exam. Mr. Handsome is the 16th mountain lion rescue for the Oakland Zoo through their Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT) alliance. While this big cat’s journey has a happy ending, not all mountain lions are as lucky. They face numerous threats in California, often struck by cars, killed with depredation permits, and by illegal poaching. articles.text: Piedmont resident, attorney Shanti Brien featured June 22 The Piedmont League of Women Voters will present a Zoom-based discussion on criminal justice reform with Piedmont resident Shanti Brien as guest speaker on June 22. An attorney and reform advocate, Brien will speak on what individuals and organizations do for criminal justice reform and racial justice. She will take questions from audience members. The forum will be online through Zoom on Tuesday, June 22 at 4 p.m. Brien’s book Almost Innocent: From searching to saved in America’s criminal justice system was published last month. It chronicles her experiences growing up in the central valley, becoming an attorney, and representing convicted individuals. Brien said that she “reimagines the current criminal justice system as smaller, fairer, and more humane.” Brien is a member of the Muscogee Creek Nation, and a graduate of UC Berkeley and Stanford Law School. As a former criminal defense lawyer, she co-founded Fogbreak Justice, an organization that collaborates with criminal justice professionals to reduce bias and build community trust to create equitable outcomes. She is also a writer and speaker on Attorney Shanti Brien social justice issues in criminal law and policy. As a Piedmont resident, she has served on the Public Safety Committee, is a member of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and participates in the Piedmont Race and Equity Campaign (PREC). To join in the discussion, register at: https://www. l w v p ie d m o n t .o r g /c o n t e n t . a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1441599. Registrants will receive an email with the Zoom link. This event is free and open to all. The talk will be recorded and can be viewed later on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube Channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg/featured.

articles.text: Early this morning, from 4:11 a.m. to 4:25 a.m., a lunar eclipse occurred, hiding the full moon in total shadow. The May 26 ultra-rare “Super Flower Blood Moon” turned a shade of red as it passed through the Earth’s umbral shadow. Blood Moons are not overly rare in themselves, but the combination of Blood Moon, Super Moon, and Flower Moon on the same night is exceedingly rare. A Super Moon is the point of the moon’s orbit when it’s at its closest to Earth and it appears up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than normal. A Flower Moon happens during springtime when the flowers are hitting their peak bloom. A Blood Moon is another name for a lunar eclipse. The celestial phenomenon was most visible from the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and Australia. articles.text: Kids have had to forgo many important rites and rituals this year. In-person learning, social activities, sports, prom – you name it. When I think about how completely abnormal this year has been for children, it is mind blowing. As a Head of School I am searching for ways to help them recover. Horrible, challenging, lonely, frustrating, sad – there are a million emotions to describe it. Take your pick. When we focus on our feelings and help our kids do the same, we embark on a dynamic journey. Going with the emotional flow inevitably allows us to move through the experience rather than being stuck in it. And this is what our children need right now. This past year was a whole bunch of things, but it wasn’t lost. Encouraging our kids to express their feelings about the experience, rather than writing it off, will allow them to come out the other side feeling empowered. Now that they’re back in school, my students are confronting their feelings about the past year, and it’s hard. But with our encouragement, they are doing it. And as they do it, little by little, they are reclaiming their former selves. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org. As we start to see the light at the end of the tunnel, and as students return to school, I see glimmers of hope. But I also see the lingering struggle, and I anticipate it will take a while before things return to normal. “It’s been a lost year,” a parent said to me recently. “And they’ll never get it back.” I’ve heard the term lost year a lot lately. It makes sense that peoThink about COVID in terms of how it felt rather than what it did or did not do to us. ple would see COVID this way after so much deprivation. But I think it’s a mistake to think about the past year as being lost, and an even bigger mistake to use this term with our kids, and here’s why. Losing a year implies nothing happened, which is untrue, and the phrase also leaves us feeling helpless. There’s literally nothing we can do to reverse the clock; there’s no option for a mulligan. The term lost also fixes the experience in our minds; it’s a definitive and static descriptor. Thinking of the past year as lost hinders our kids’ ability to process the experience because it keeps them focused on what happened, or what didn’t happen, or on what they can’t change. This breeds helplessness. Thinking about COVID in terms of how it felt is another story.
articles.title: Going with the flow of feelings

articles.text: How other local churches are offering services Piedmont Community Church welcomed church-goers for in-person worship on May 16 for the first time in over a year. The church has been closed for in-person worship and has relied on digital, live-streamed services since March 2020 due to the global health pandemic and subsequent industry closures. Currently, the Piedmont Community Church is welcoming parishioners at about half capacity - or approximately 75 people total. It requires masks and social distancing. Still, pews were “at capacity,” and reservations filled up prior to the first in-person Sunday service. May 16 also marked the first in-person worship service for Transitional Minister Dr. Steve Schibsted, who joined the church in the midst of the global pandemic. In his sermon Dr. Schibsted described the theme as a “perfect storm,” referencing the Bible text of Jesus’ walk on water, and the 2001 George Clooney film of the same name. “We just experienced a perfect storm, or a confluence of storms. It’s easy to think of the pandemic as one [factor], but we’ve been through an economic downturn, social upheaval, racial injustices, and our country coming faceto-face with the racism that still exists,” Dr. Schibsted said. His first live sermon carried a theme of hope and of transition. Piedmont Community Church will continue with modified, in-person worship services for the next three weeks and will maintain virtual services. The state and county have not given guidance for how to operate in-person worship services beyond June 15, at which time the state’s color-coded “tier” system is expected to disappear. Gov. Gavin Newsom said that on June 15 California will fully open its economy if vaccine supply is sufficient and hospitalization rates are stable and low. Dr. Schibsted said that given the fluctuating nature of regulations, it is hard to say what worship services will look like past the current tier system. “We’re thinking that by June 15 things will be very different. What that means exactly, I Piedmont Community Church wouldn’t want to speculate,” he said. Sunday services begin at 10:30 a.m., and reservations are required. Services will include liturgical readings with response, music, and a sermon. Reservations can be made for May 30, June 6, and June 13 by visiting https://www.piedmontchurch.org/ reopening/. Michael Barber, Communications Director for Piedmont Community Church, explained that the church will continue live-streaming worship services. “We began live streaming services in 2018. Our online worship has been pre-produced since March of 2020. Going forward, we will continue to provide online worship for our parishioners, and the 30% of our online audience that live outside the state,” he said. “However, we are looking at ways to combine the live worship experience with the highly produced content to which our online audience has become accustomed.” Corpus Christi Catholic Church St. James Drive, Piedmont Indoor services are available. Saturday Vigil services at 6 p.m., weekday mass is at 9 a.m., and Sunday mass is at 9 a.m. and 11 a.m. Masks must be worn, and parishioners are asked to remain 6-feet apart from others in pews, unless accompanied by another member of your household. Once communion is received, you can lower your mask to consume the Eucharist. Drive-through Communion is every Sunday, from 10:45 to 11:15 am. Zion continues to Live Stream the Sunday Services every Sunday at 8:30 am and 11:00 am. articles.text: 11-7 loss to Miramonte; defeated Washington 19-1 The PHS boys’ lacrosse team split its last two matches, losing to non-league Miramonte 11-7 on Saturday afternoon, May 22 in Orinda, while pounding Washington 19-1 at Witter Field one day earlier. The Highlanders Playing the Castro Valley Trojans, Piedmont posted a commanding 77-59 win. articles.text: Piedmont High School welcomed back an official interscholastic sport in 2021 to Binks Rawlings Gym after a 20-year absence. The boys’ volleyball team, expansion team in the Western Alameda County Conference, beat Encinal 3-1 on Tuesday, May 25 by scores of 22-25, 25-20, 25-12, and 26-24. “The old boys’ volleyball team disbanded 20-some years ago. Interest in the sport picked up back in middle school. We were set to start last but we only played one match before the pandemic,” said a sophomore captain Wilson Wong. The school finished the 1999 season as the No. 3 seed in the NCS Tournament, falling to No. 2 Campolindo 3-0 in the semifinals on May 20, 1999, exactly 21 years ago. The volleyball team finished the 20th century with a successful 16-5 overall record, but was never heard from again. That was until Wong and the current members of the team began a middle school club that formed into a full-fledged team for the high school. They officially entering the WACC in 2020 prior to the pandemic. “It feels like we’re a part of something bigger by helping the sport grow at the school. We didn’t think we’d play volleyball again after middle school, but our group of guys wasn’t ready to stop. I got in contact with people, went to meetings and collected the players. Now we’re here, playing, and having fun,” explained Wong. The team has 11 players: Wong, sophomore Owen Kelly, sophomore Ryan McConathy, sophomore Brayden Day, junior Patrick Alexandre, sophomore Kai Lambert, sophomore Romen Meima, freshman Danny Allen, freshman Shunji Higashi, freshman John Champion, and sophomore Eric Olaru-Hagen. The Highlanders defeated Tennyson on Tuesday, May 18 in a narrow 3-2 contest by scores of 21-25, 25-19, 25-21, 22-25, and 16-14. “We lack experience, but we can swing momentum. We have a lot of fire. We know that we’re undersized [and less experienced], but if we really get going, we can bring out the skill,” explained Wong. In their first year with three wins and teetering on the edge of a .500 win percentage, the players have reason to be proud. 2021 has been a terrific start, and with a team of 11 potential returners for 2022, the future is certainly bright. “We have a lot of potential. Next year, we’ll have a longer season and a lot of experience playing together. We hope to push people to play for clubs outside of the school,” said Wong. Textures, color and organic forms are layered into a complex visual weave that hints at the underlying feelings and complexity of our lives. Paula moved with her family from Santiago, Chile to Piedmont in 2013. She has a studio in the Industrial Center Building in Sausalito. www.Paulavalenzuelaart.com Paula Valenzuela Paula Valenzuela is a Chilean abstract artist based in Piedmont. Her work explores the connection of darkness and light within us, the complexity of layers that we show to others and to ourselves. As an artist and psychotherapist, Valenzuela is interested in the cycles of the human experience, specially the internal and spiritual transformations between the birthing and dying processes. Her work is inspired by the colors of the desert, constellations, internal experiences and collective symbols. He paints mostly with locally made watercolors and handcrafted inks foraged from pigments found in the Bay Area. His handmade inks range from sycamore bark, rust, black walnuts, and oxalis leaves found in his neighborhood to library pencils and a charred copy of Fahrenheit 451. Deeply observational, his work focuses on amplifying small moments in the world around us. Mike’s work is usually large scale paintings, with an emphasis on surface texture & darker, warmer color palettes. articles.text: A scene from the documentary Maiden. Maiden is the name of a boat helmed by an all-female crew that entered what was then called the Whitbread Round the World Race, a sailing competition that began in September 1989 and would not finish until May 1990. This race (perhaps “ordeal” is a better word) departed from South Hampton, England, on the first leg to Punta Del Este, Uruguay; then on to Fremantle, Australia; next Aukland, New Zealand; back to Punta Del Este; then Ft. Lauderdale, Florida; and finally a long return to South Hampton. The distance covered was some 45,000 nautical miles across and through some of the most grueling and harrowing sailing conditions imaginable. It was a test of will and tenacity that challenges the edges of a sailor’s abilities and all but defies the imagination. At the center of this race was Tracy Edwards who, after being denied berths on boats slated to enter the competition, and coming to realize that yacht racing was viewed as a man’s world, decided to mortgage her home, find a second-hand boat, and assemble an all-female crew with a plan to enter the 1989 Whitbread – an effort viewed as being against all odds. The boat was a fixer-upper that needed stem to stern retrofitting. As well, Tracy was desperate to find sponsorship and funding. Ultimately, King Hussein of Jordan stepped forward and offered to underwrite the Maiden’s entry. To Tracy’s relief, her crew proved to be a startling resilient group of women who refused to yield. Ironically, Tracy herself, despite her patina of resolve and courage, proved, at times to be the most fragile. Clearly the yachting world in 1989 was male dominated. The Maiden’s entry was met with unvarnished skepticism, if not outright hostility from dry land experts, blue water sailors, and a nautical press that would follow closely every leg of the race. Nevertheless, Edwards and the women carried on. Initially, much of the press coverage bordered on the misogynistic. But eventually Maiden was given some faint praise, and finally awarded a grudging acknowledgment of what they were in the process of achieving. The crew and Edwards herself proved to be a committed group of fierce competitors. And a more apt name for their boat might have been Defiant, for that is what they were all about. Despite yachting’s glass ceiling, they never yielded. During the leg to Auckland, the boat began to take on water, due in part to a leak around the mast. The problem delayed them 18 hours. The most harrowing days were after leaving Punta Del Este and sailing around the tip of South America. The deck was covered in snow and ice and the ocean a spray of freezing water and pounding, surging waves. It was a test of their grit and steadfastness and ultimate determination as well as a test of endurance and survival for the women and the boat. Edwards does say, looking back, she didn’t realize she had entered a battle until she was in it, one against not just the ocean, but also the chauvinistic world of yachting. When asked if she was a feminist, she said “no.” She later clarified that she merely wanted to engage in a race that fully captured her spirit and desire. “I’d begun a fight I didn’t realize I was having,” she said upon reflection. Maiden is a sea tale that is both electric and riveting, yet it also feels incomplete. The 16mm film had the feel, in parts, of a home movie with voice-over and interviews with crew members and Edwards. But there was so much that could not be covered and that needed more time and description – something that can only be conveyed through a tightly written screenplay with actors at the helm. The Maiden won two legs of its race, a remarkable feat given the circumstances of its entry into the Whitbread. Also remarkable is this account of an unforgettable and compelling race, a race that reveals a most surprising and wonderful final return to South Hampton. Maiden . Documentar y. Directed by Alex Holmes. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Director-Screenwriter Yorgos Lanthimos won the European Film Award for Best Screenwriter in 2015 for The Lobster. The Lobster dribbled into theaters in 2015 to an initial reception of dumbfoundedness and confusion. Filmed in Ireland, this surreal, black comedy loosely aims at satire. Greek Director Yorgos Lanthimos takes the viewer to a dystopian society where everyone must be married or else they are forced to be transfigured into an animal of their choice. Colin Farrell stars as the protagonist, David. After his wife leaves him, he is taken to a lastditch hotel designated for matching up singles. He chooses to be transformed into a lobster if he cannot find a suitable mate. In brutal, dead-pan fashion, he tells the hotel manager (Olivia Colman) that lobsters remain fertile for life, have blue blood like aristocrats, and that “he quite likes the sea.” The Lobster may be too weird for some. Though it’s a comedy, there may not be a single chuckle of laughter by any of the actors in the film. I recommend that you give it a go, maybe even watch it a second time with the subtitles on. It’s a head scratcher but also a movie that requires thought well outside the box office. In the story, adults who become single or have just graduated from high school are taken to the fancy resort to find a new companion within 45 days. The only way to extend your stay is to shoot and capture one of the “loners” in the woods with a tranquilizer dart. Each captured loner buys you one more day at the hotel and prolongs your dating misadventure. The single people doomed to become dogs, ponies, or peacocks preoccupy themselves with the notion that they must match themselves up with someone with similar physical flaws, like frequent nose bleeds or a limp. Such oddities riddle the movie, and “the bizarre” becomes the resounding motif. Some viewers may be frustrated by these “holes” in the plot line, but they serve as a commentary on dating society with poignancy. John C. Reily (Talladega Nights, Step Brothers) has a lisp and awaits for a woman also with a lisp to arrive at the hotel. The film offers no explanation for why the characters are convinced that physical deficiencies are the key to love. Other than suggesting there are no rules in love or war. If you’re looking for something different, check it out. It is available at Piedmont Avenue’s Video Room. In 2015 The Lobster had a slow opening weekend, grossing only $50,000. Since then, the film has all the elements of becoming a cult classic. The Lobster. Directed by Yorgos Lanthimos. Starring Colin Farrell, John C. Reily, Rachel Weisz and Olivia Coleman. 119 minutes. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Zootopia. Zootopia is not your typical animated talking animals movie; rather, Disney created a family-friendly buddy cop comedy with a raft of subtle messages and teachable moments. The film is set in a world where predator and prey identities have been abolished, hence Zootopia (utopia). The story focuses on Judy Hopp (Ginnifer Goodwin), the first metropolitan bunny cop ever hired. She’s a perky go-getter and determined to prove herself. But on her first day on the force, to her surprise, she confronts some discouraging prejudices. Given her size, and given some thick-headed assumptions, officer Hopps is assigned parking ticket duty by her Cape Buffalo police chief, Bogo (Idris Elba). But then Judy learns that a family man, Mr. Otter, has disappeared and his wife, Mrs. Otter, is frantic, and appeals to Judy to help find him. Judy rises to the challenge and bets her career that she can. The problem is that in order to track down Mr. Otter she will have to partner up with slick and sly fox, Nick Wilde (Jason Bateman), which forces her to rethink her assumptions about foxes in general. The team’s search for the missing Mr. O. takes the pair in unexpected directions, while encountering a most extraordinary cast of characters, including an adorable lamb, a mafia-type polar bear, and a wonderful sloth who works for the Department of Motor Vehicles, guaranteeing extremely slow service and long, exasperating lines. Judy and Nick must also unravel an unanticipated conspiracy, one that tests their teamA scene from Disney’s Zootopia.

There are also moments of silly slapstick, exciting chases, all while taking them into fascinating enclaves of Zootopia known as Tundra Town, Sahara Square, and Little Rodentia. For all of the film’s asides, and some not too subtle references to Disney’s Frozen, the most significant are the scenes that touch on racism in everyday Zootopian life. Hopps, for example, makes the point that “cute” is a word used only by bunnies and considered offensive if used by other denizens of Zootopia. What Disney points out, often with the lightest of touches, is that we are all tempted to prejudge one another, even by the benign Judy Hopps. However, when Judy is confronted by her blind spots regarding Zootopians, she willingly steps up and apologizes to those she has offended and promises to do better. All of this takes place in the context of a fun, exiting movie with lots of laughs and energetic, fast-paced animation that pays close attention to detail and texture. Zootopia. Disney animation. articles.text: Reading George Lang’s cookbook, Cuisine of Hungary, will bring a smile to your face. It reads more like an historical novel than a cookbook. Hungarian music is very communicative. Everyone knows Brahms’ Hungarian dances, and Liszt’s Hungarian rhapsodies. This music has entertained millions of people through cartoons for almost 100 years. But there is more to Hungary than Brahms’ Hungarian Dance No. 5 or Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2. When considering the cuisines of the world, Hungary is hardly ever mentioned. For sheer numbers, Chinese and Indian food must rank at the top. French cuisine is the touchstone for the rest of the world. The interesting thing is that French cuisine is the stepchild of Italian cuisine. When Catherine de Medici became the queen of France by marrying King Henry II in 1533, she brought her chefs from Florence. The French then did the thing which they do so well – take credit for whatever you can. The United States is famous for its international restaurants, but there are precious few Hungarian restaurants on the list. This is a shame because Hungarian cuisine is fabulous. I discovered George Lang’s cookbook, Cuisine of Hungary, a few days ago and to say that it makes good reading is an understatement. Lang is a brilliant writer. Even though this is a cookbook, it reads like a great novel. He includes the entire history of Hungary and its neighbors geopolitically and gastronomically. Along the way you get some wry humor and valuable cooking tips. It includes some bits of philosophy as well. An example: “Every small nation must be chauvinistic in order to survive. There was a Hungarian professor who carried chauvinism to the extreme by trying to show that everything originated in Hungary, including paradise.” Then Lang goes into the history of Hungarian cabbage recipes. Reading it will bring a smile to your face. When he gives readers his recipes for making goulash, he takes neighbor Romania to task. He says that most of the things that pass for goulash aren’t very good. What is usually served as goulash shouldn’t happen to a Romanian, he asserts. To be fair, Hungarian food is sometimes a bit heavy. Lard is the omnipresent ingredient. Hungarian Jews used chicken fat instead of lard. After you have enjoyed a very good Hungarian main course, be sure to let your imagination run wild with desserts. While the French take credit for many desserts, the readers will be surprised to know that the Hungarians were first to create desserts. After dinner have some Tokay wine. Under Communism in Hungary, the best Tokay wine was exported. With this book, prepare to have some fun with history and cuisine. For music listen to the Liszt Hungarian Rhapsodies as played by the superlative pianist Georges Cziffra. For sheer genius, listen to Vladimir Horowitz play his version of the Second Hungarian Rhapsody. And for nostalgia listen to my old friend Shony Alex Braun play Hungarian Gypsy favorites. Pretend that you are in a romantic restaurant in old Budapest.

articles.text: On view: Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes” The San Jose Museum of Art (SJMA) is open to the public on weekends, Friday through Sunday. Currently on view are Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes.” White’s “Noisy Blushes” (2020) serves as a meditation on movement and time, light and color; as well as actual material presence and form. The artwork was commissioned by the San Jose Museum of Art; it fills the building’s 39-foot high atrium to transform the entrance for visitors. Another sculpture on display is Do Ho Suh’s “Karma,” a 23-foot tower of bronze male figures perched on top of each other’s shoulders and shielding that figure’s eyes with his hands. “Karma” will be on display through January 30, 2022. There are exhibitions for youth as well. The Koret Gallery and Art Learning Lab is an exhibition space inspired by sensory learning, and promotes creative exploration by children age 12 and younger. The museum’s multi-award winning STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art and Math) education program features a diverse selection of artworks from the permanent collection. Through interactive play, young visitors are encouraged to draw their own connections between individual creative exploration using various tools and mediums. “We have been hard at work investing in a better SJMA for a stronger post-pandemic Museum,“ said Executive Director Sayre Batton. We continue internal work to become an anti-racist museum with allday trainings on building racial Art installation in the Atrium at the San Jose Museum of Art. equity that tie into our strategic goal to discuss issues and places for change.” The museum is restricting large groups and has temporarily cancelled group tours. Individuals, and small cohorts of visitors, are welcome to view exhibitions and artist highlights that are on gallery walls. All volunteers, docents, staff, and visitors must wear a mask or face covering and observe physical distancing guidelines. The museum is open Friday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the first hour dedicated to seniors, women who are pregnant, and those with underlying health concerns. SJMA offers free admission for youth, college students, and teachers. To obtain tickets, visit https:// sjmusart.org/.

articles.text: Filoli House and Garden is celebrating the LGBTQ community with a weekend of history and art on Saturday and Sunday, June 5 and 6. Visit the garden in Woodside any time between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. Visitors can embark on a colorful journey on the iconic pride flag through Filoli’s Estate Trail. The trail is transformed into a rainbow walk; at each station, you will learn about the meaning of each color in the flag. A “soundscape” will be offered on the Garden House lawn, where visitors will have the opportunity to hear about the progress that has been made in the fight for equality, the people who have advocated for such, and what’s still left to be done. Stunning floral arrangements will take over the gardens, created by the Nigella botanical boutique team in San Francisco. Visitors will learn more about the company’s connection to the LGBTQ community. Specialty drinks and treats will be sold from Little Green Cycle under the shade of the olive groves between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. Summer Nights at Filoli Pride weekend also coincides with Filoli’s “Summer Nights” series of events, which begin tomorrow, May 27, and run through the end of September. Come dressed in your most extravagant Dynasty lookalike outfit on Thursday, June 3 from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. Some will remember that Filoli House served as the mansion on the popular Dynasty TV show about the goings-on of a wealthy Denver family. The show spanned a decade in the 80s and helped pioneer compelling narratives around gender inequality and featured prime time’s first openly gay character and first Black female lead. Numerous scenes were filmed at Filoli, including the series pilot. Visit https://filoli.org/pride/ for ticketing information. Celebrate Pride month will be saluted by Filoli House and Garden the weekend of June 5-6.
articles.title: Celebrate Pride at Filoli Garden June 5 and 6

articles.text: Archived SF Jazz performances available through June The San Francisco Jazz Festival will begin on June 3 as a virtual festival. First launched as a two-day festival in 1983, the San Francisco Jazz Festival is the foundational annual June concert event upon which the organization SF Jazz was built. The festival will present a virtual edition of programming, to include 18 exclusive broadcasts that will feature highlights from past performances, world premiere concerts, a rare film documentary on Thelonious Monk, events honoring Juneteenth, and more. SF Jazz utilizes its extensive archives and presents a hybrid of the annual June jazz festival, with virtual performances by vocalist Jazzmeia Horn, drummer Brian Blade, The Harold Lopez-Nussa Quartet saxophonist Melissa Aldana, and pianist Harold Lopez-Nussa from Havana. On T hu rsd ay, Ju ne 3, Lopez-Nussa’s quartet will perform live from Havana at 7 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ for information on how to reserve a spot for the live-stream performance. Through the month of June, SF Jazz will present a total of 18 concerts, both archival and live-streamed performances. For a full lineup, visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/sfjazz-digital/ virtual-san-francisco-jazz-festival-2021/.
articles.title: San Francisco virtual jazz festival begins June 3

articles.text: The kitchen is often the hub of the home. It’s no wonder a kitchen remodel has some homeowners leaving their home until the work is done. But if that’s not part of the plan or budget, you can survive a kitchen remodel with a little preparation. You’ll want to work with a contractor who values your schedule to minimize disruptions to family routines. Here are a few of our sanity-saving tips to prepare any area of your home for construction. Create a “Safe Zone” – Designate a room to store temporarily displaced items. Pack fragile and valuable items like fine china, photos, artwork, electronics, etc. and move it to the “safe zone.” Define “Work Zone” – Define where workers are allowed, and not allowed in your home. We recommend ZipWalling these areas off from the rest of the house. Define “Time Zone” – Define when workers are allowed to work or visit before construction begins. Always wear shoes – Take precautions to protect yourself when walking around a construction zone. Keep a Positive Attitude – This too shall pass – and we hope the results are worth it. Construction is dusty work, but with a little preparation your home can stay relatively dustfree. Here are a few techniques any contractor should employ to minimize dust exposure: Dust barriers and ZipWalls – Install plastic sheets over doorways and openings to create a barrier to non-construction areas. Air filtration – Reduce dust by drawing in particulate laden air and filtering it, before venting outdoors. Power tools with dust extractors – Employ tools with built-in dust extractors to further minimize dust and debris. Sticky mats and floor paper – Place at entries to remove dirt from tracking in and out and to protect flooring and carpet. Now for the biggest concern: Cooking during a kitchen remodel Consider remodeling your kitchen during the summer or fall when the weather allows for outdoor cooking and grilling. Areas to set up a temporary kitchen can include: the garage, patio, deck, or even your front porch. Here are our tips for keeping you fed when your kitchen turns into a construction zone. Set up a temporary kitchen – Pack up your kitchen in advance, reserving minimal items for your temporary kitchen. Set up a wash station – Designate a room with a sink as the temporary wash station. Bring out your camp cook – Normalize camp food and prepare hot meals using your gas grill, electric skillet or propane stove, for a reliable heat source. ZipWall barrier will help to keep dust out of the rest of your home during construction. Get a mini-fridge – A minifridge gives you easy access to store perishables while construction is underway. You can ask your contractor to move your fridge to a temporary location and move it back when the job is done. Create a temporary countertop – Get a foldable table for countertop space to fit a microwave, electric kettle, or a cutting board. And lastly, factor in the costs of dining out in your overall budget, because you will have to eat out occasionally! Now, you’re all set for a successful kitchen remodeling project. If you need more tips, contact us at hdrremodeling.com. Kevin Mond is head of project development at HDR Remodeling, 2952 Sacramento St, Berkeley. Tel. 510-845-6100. hdrremodeling.com. articles.text: Many may not yet be aware that there’s a vibrant art and food scene right in our backyard. It’s happening on 25th Street between Broadway and Telegraph in Uptown Oakland. This exciting creative community includes art galleries as well as studios where sculptors, painters, artisans, fashion designers, and jewelers, practice their craft. Galleries include Slate Contemporary, Mercury 20, Local Language, Manna, the Fourth Wall, Applied Contemporary. Werkshack, and FM Oakland have gallery spaces as well as studios. While weekday hours vary, Saturday afternoons are a time when you can guarantee that all of the visual art venues on 25th Street will have their doors open for “Saturday Stroll.” If you are interested in a free, guided walking-tour of 25th street’s art spaces, including a special opening for the Gold show at the Werkshack, send an e-mail info@slateart.net to sign up for a tour led by Danielle Fox of Slate Contemporary Gallery on Saturday, June 12 at 2:00 pm. If her name is familiar, it’s because she is one of the two judges of the recent Juried Art Show at the Piedmont center for the Arts. Food and beverage businesses on the block are generally open Thursday and Friday evenings, and all day and evening on Saturday. The businesses on 25th Street include Forage Kitchen, Hofkuche Beer Garden, Friends and Family Bar, and Oakland Spirits Co. – all of which have outdoor seating. Depending when you drop in, you might be able to hear live music from The John Brothers Piano Company at Oakland Spirit Company, while enjoying wines made on site, unique cocktails, and hot empanadas. Hofkuche, a German Sausage, Schnitzel, and Beer Garden, will be hosting Trivia Night on Third Thursdays this summer, plus art Slate Gallery on 25th Street in Oakland. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers stop for a group photo halfway up Scenic Avenue at the Eliassen Overlook. Pictured are (front): Cheryl Coleman Jones (left) and Sherry Jacobs; (back) Albert Chen, Nancy Henn, Kat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Brenda Ferrero, Melba Yee, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. The members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoy walking to seldom seen places in Piedmont. The hidden pathways and stairs around the city provide this opportunity. On a recent walk, the group had experienced the short 89-foot path between Piedmont Court and Mountain Avenue. This past Wednesday, May 19, they were interested in seeing more similar paths. Twelve members of the group assembled at the Exedra on a mild morning. On hand were Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kuo, Adrienne Hamlin, Susan Martin, Albert Chen, Kat and Bob Gustafson, Nancy Henn, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome first-time walker Cheryl Coleman Jones. The group was up for a bit of a challenge. They learned from a summary in a past issue of Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society magazine that there are 21 paths in Piedmont, the longest of which is the 281-foot set of stairs that links Scenic and Blair Avenues. In fact, there are two other stair pathways on Scenic; two fewer than St. James which has the most in the city with four stairway paths. Strong winds the night before had helped clean the air, so the walkers thought the views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco would be good from Scenic Avenue, an appropriate name. The group departed from the Exedra on Highland Avenue to Pala Avenue and up to Mesa Avenue. The group has an informal objective of walking every safe Piedmont street during the year. Going on Mesa to Moraga, then back on Monte Avenue one block away allowed the walkers to color in a set of streets on their Piedmont map. The route allowed them to see the lovely homes on these streets, and they particularly liked a beautiful Victorian on Mesa and what they believe is a Julia Morgan designed home on Pala. articles.text: Michael Cavenaugh passed away peacefully on May 1, 2021, at his home in Walnut Creek with his family at his side. Up to his last days, he remained joyful and happy, always with his sense of humor. He was 88. Born Michael Frederick Cavenaugh on November 17, 1932, he was the son of Harry Taylor Cavenaugh and Ruth (Andrews) Cavenaugh of Yonkers, New York. His mother performed on Broadway before passing away at the age of 39 from pneumonia in 1941. After his mother’s death, Mike was sent to boarding school as his father struggled with the loss of his wife. Mike inherited her gift of music. As an organist he could play any song by ear. Years later, every day after work Mike would sit at his organ and play. He found joy in the music that warmed the house every evening. After high school, he joined the Air Force. One year later he earned admission to the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, New York. He graduated from West Point in 1956 as the fourth generation of the Cavenaugh family to do so. During his six years in the military, he was an expert marksman and served as a general’s aide while stationed in Panama, South America, and Korea. He also served in the Old Guard in Washington, D.C., and had the distinction of leading the Inaugural Parade for President John F. Kennedy. His time at West Point shaped his life, which was built on hard work, honesty and integrity. He was known as a true gentleman, kind to strangers, gentle, warm and always with a great sense of humor that he seemed to enjoy as much as anyone. He left the Army in 1962, and longed for a traditional family life which he had missed since age nine. He joined Merrill Lynch as a financial advisor in 1962 in Baltimore, Maryland. In September he answered an ad for a rental apartment, then occupied by Frances Glass from North Wilkesboro. There he met a charming Southern redhead full of energy and donning a big smile. She was making plans to move to New York. The two of them talked for three hours that day. Afterward, Fran called her friend and said she had met the man she was going to marry, despite not even knowing his name. He clearly felt the connection and knocked on her door one week later. Two years later, on September 5, 1964, they were married Mike was with Merrill Lynch for 35 years and he retired in 1997. He missed only one day of work in three decades due to illness. He worked with good friends Bob Sanford and Steve Griswold and almost daily had lunch with them while playing pinball. Watching Mike play pinball was a spectacle as he energetically made it an aerobic exercise. Mike was a loving husband and father. He and Fran lived most of their lives in Baltimore, where their children, Lisa and Dan, attended Roland Park Country School and Gilman, respectively. Mike was an avid tennis player and played five days a week until he was 84. He was also a great dancer, an occasional artist (including stained glass), a lifelong genealogist, a restorer of antique cars, and a regular handyman. Perhaps his greatest passion though was his family. It was rare to have a conversation with him when he was not fawning over Fran as the one and only love of his life. His lavish praise was also spent on his children, where he always saw the best in them. To talk of his life and leave out his warm sense of humor would be the grandest of oversights. He was a lover of Peter Seller’s movies and would often start laughing while telling jokes before others could even understand or appreciate the punchline. During his last moment of consciousness, he tried to tell a joke with a twinkle in his eye. Mike was also an incredibly patient man and full of great advice. He shouldered the role of the family patriarch in his 20s, providing both thoughtful counsel and financial support to his father and brothers. He did so out Michael Cavenaugh at West Point in 1956. Michael Cavenaugh died on May 1 at age 88. of love and his belief that there was nothing more important than family. His love of family expanded to embrace Fran’s mother and father in North Carolina. During their trips to North Wilkesboro, he would spend his days working on the home of his in-laws, Mansfield and Novel Glass. He could also be found at the local library investigating the family history, talking to cousins, aunts and uncles to soak up everything there was to know about his extended family. With family always a priority, Mike and Fran daringly moved to California in 2004 to be closer to their grandchildren. Mike helped his son fix up their new home in Piedmont, where he loved his house projects. In his last seven years as he dealt with dementia, he remained joyful and happy. Fran cared for him every step of the way, along with help from his daughter in their home in Rossmoor. Mike had a life of rich memories. His favorite saying was “Life is a Collection of Memories.” By that measure Michael Frederick Cavenaugh had a life better than he could have imagined as a young man…a family, a home, a love. His last words to Fran were, “I’m happy.” He is survived by his loving wife of over 56 years, Frances Rebecca (Glass) Cavenaugh; daughter Lisa; son Dan; daughter-in-law Jennifer (Smith); and grandchildren Jackson, Salem and Shelby. Michael is predeceased by his brothers, Alan and Harry Cavenaugh. The family will have a private memorial service in June at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Hospice East Bay (hospiceeastbay.org). The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary.
